terms.meaning: A uniform mixture of two or more substances.
The solid that dissolves, or the liquid in smaller amount.
The liquid that a solid dissolves in, or the liquid in larger amount.
No more solute can dissolve at that temperature.
More solute can still dissolve at that temperature.
The most solute that can dissolve in a fixed amount, 100 mL, at a given temperature.
The mass in a unit volume of a substance.
The curved surface of a liquid in a measuring cylinder.

items.name: Which part is the solvent?
items.formula: In a solid dissolved in a liquid, the liquid is always the solvent.
items.example: In thick sugar syrup, water is still the solvent, though there is more sugar.

items.name: Air as a solution
items.formula: Nitrogen is the solvent. Oxygen, argon and carbon dioxide are solutes.
items.example: Nitrogen is present in the largest amount.

items.name: Temperature and solids
items.formula: Solids generally dissolve more as temperature rises.
items.example: A saturated sugar solution becomes unsaturated when heated.

items.name: Temperature and gases
items.formula: Gases dissolve less as temperature rises.
items.example: Warm water holds less oxygen, which is hard on fish.

items.name: Formula for density
items.example: 54 g of aluminium with volume 20 cm³: 54 ÷ 20 = 2.7 g/cm³

items.name: Units of density
items.formula: SI unit: kg/m³. In the lab: g/cm³. Water is about 1 g/cm³.

items.name: Relative density
items.formula: Density of the substance ÷ Density of water. It has no unit.

items.name: Floating and sinking
items.formula: Less dense than water: floats. More dense: sinks.
items.example: Oil and wood float. Iron and stone sink.

items.name: Layers of the Earth
items.formula: Arranged by density, with the lightest crust on top and the densest core at the centre.

items.name: Volume of a stone
items.formula: Volume = Final level − Initial level in a measuring cylinder.
items.example: 65 mL − 50 mL = 15 mL, so the stone’s volume is 15 cm³.

items.name: Reading a measuring cylinder
items.formula: Water and clear liquids: read the bottom of the curve. Coloured liquids: read the top.
items.example: Keep your eye level with the mark.

items.name: Heating and density
items.formula: Heating generally makes a substance expand, so its density falls.
items.example: This is why hot air rises in a hot air balloon.

items.name: Water at 4 °C
items.formula: Water is densest at 4 °C. Ice is less dense, so it floats.
items.example: The ice on a frozen lake keeps the water below it liquid for the fish.

items.name: Pressure and density
items.formula: Pressure raises the density of a gas greatly, but it has little effect on liquids and solids.
items.example: Air can be squeezed into a small tyre.

mistakes.text: Heat helps solids to dissolve but makes gases dissolve less. Do not use one rule for both.
Relative density has no unit, because it is a ratio.
A big object is not always denser. A heavy log floats while a small iron nail sinks.
Water does not get steadily denser all the way down to freezing. Below 4 °C its density falls.
